title: Alice began on a rowing boat
hook: Alice in Wonderland was first told aloud on a summer boat trip near Oxford.
peek: On 4 July 1862, an Oxford maths lecturer rowed three young sisters up the Thames and made up a story to pass the time. One of the girls, Alice Liddell, asked him to write it down. The result was Alice's Adventures in Wonderland.
lede: On 4 July 1862, Charles Dodgson, an Oxford mathematics lecturer, rowed up the Thames from Folly Bridge towards Godstow with his friend Robinson Duckworth and three sisters: Lorina, Alice and Edith Liddell. To entertain the girls, he made up a story about a girl called Alice who fell down a rabbit hole. Ten-year-old Alice begged him to write it down.

bullets.text: Dodgson spent many months writing out the story by hand and drawing his own pictures. He gave the finished notebook, called Alice's Adventures Under Ground, to Alice as an early Christmas present in 1864.
The book's opening poem remembers the trip as a hot, golden summer afternoon on the river. Weather records suggest the day was in fact cool and damp. Memory, or poetry, seems to have improved it.
Dodgson published the expanded book in 1865 as Lewis Carroll, a playful twist on his first two names, Charles Lutwidge. John Tenniel drew the illustrations that most readers still picture.
The handwritten notebook was sold by Alice in 1928 and went to America. In 1948 a group of American donors bought it and gave it back to Britain, and it is now in the British Library.
